#### **Introduction** 

**•**<sup>**_December has started with an air of hope,_**</sup> **_following the moves from major central banks and a series of improved US economic numbers, along with the Chinese gover

nment’s shift towards monetary easing. This has given a boost to all the precious metals. Silver and the PGMs are looking for an improved industrial outlook, while the gold market is focusing on inflation. There is also a legacy of fear that the recent moves may not be enough to stave off further crises._** **•****_After a sharp correction in mid-November_** **_gold has resumed its uptrend in all the major currencies. However, jewellery demand remains patchy, but investment and, importantly for sentiment, net official sector buying interest, remains strong. Indications of increased injections of liquidity into the financial markets point to heightened fears of inflation and negative real interest rates; we expect gold to continue to strengthen and to challenge $2,000 in the second quarter of next year._** **•****_Silver is likely to continue to underperform_** **_gold. **I1** Economic Indicators - December 2011 ##### **The United States; green shoots of recovery but fears of smothering from the EU** While the primary focus in the media has for some weeks been on the state of the Eurozone’s financial system, the United States has been posting a series of economic figures that point towards a tentative recovery. The Chinese economy, meanwhile, has been slowing sufficiently to prompt the Chinese government into a shift in monetary stance. This development in Chinese policy, combined with the concerted actions on the part of the Federal Reserve with the Banks of Canada, England, Japan, Switzerland and the European Central Bank to reduce the cost of dollar swaps (see pages Au1 and Au3 for an account of the technicalities of the dollar swaps) have all combined to rejuvenate the spirit in the financial markets, including the commodities sector. Part of the improvement in commodity prices was due to the weakening in the dollar that followed the news of the joint action from these central banks, as the markets’ appetite for risk improved. The improvement in the euro was partly due to short-covering activity, but sentiment towards the euro remains cautious. This is another element fuelling the rejuvenation in appetite for gold as investors continue to hedge against the perceived risks in exposure to fiat currencies. As we note in the Gold chapter of this publication, this is underscored by the latest figures relating to the official sector, which show continued and accelerating interest in gold as a means of diversifying risk. Gold bounced by almost $50 in just two hours on 30th November following the announcement of the co-ordinated central bank action, although the speed of that short term move at end-November was undoubtedly increased by short-covering. Gold enters December in a relatively buoyant mood. The price action of October and November suggests that gold has formed an important band of support between $1,650 and $1,680. The risks inherent in the heady mix of sustained problems over the Eurozone, the action of the central bankers to try and aid the ailing financial system and the belief that t

he Chinese government may now be entering a phase of fiscal relaxation, all point to scope for further gains in the near future and gold could easily trade above $1,800 during December before moving towards $2,000 in the first half of 2012. These are not the only supportive features in the market; others include the continued gold purchases by the official sector and we believe that central banks will add 400500 tonnes to their reserves this year. Private investment remains strong, and although the jewellery market is still under some pressure, investment is taking up the momentum. ETF investors have also now started absorbing gold again, while the net investor long on Comex has been fluctuating. Short covering has been in evidence, although the price fall in late November (see below) was accompanied by sizeable long liquidation. There are still bouts of scrap flow in the physical market and although the general mood among private investors is bullish, sharp upward moves are likely to prompt further scrap sales in some regions. ##### **Recent price action and background financial developments** After the sharp drop in gold’s price in September and the period of consolidation between $1,600 and $1,680 in the first weeks of October, gold started a rally in the second half of that month that took it to an intraday high of just over $1,802 on 8th November. After a brief period of sideways trading, the falls in the commodity sector in mid-November took gold down towards $1,660 where more support developed.
